A head sculpt from blockout to finish

The likeness lives in the planes, not the pores. This is the pass order I use for a ZBrush head: blockout, primary forms, secondary forms, then the surface - and why getting the brow and the jaw right early saves the whole sculpt later.

1. Blockout: the skull before the face

Most failed sculpts are failed blockouts. Before any feature, the skull has to be right - the cranial mass, the angle of the jaw, the distance between the orbits. Working with a low-resolution sphere and the Move brush, the goal is a head that still reads correctly as a silhouette. If the silhouette is wrong, no amount of detail will rescue it.

  • Cranial mass - the back of the skull is usually too small.
  • Jaw angle - the single strongest identifier in a face.
  • Orbit spacing - set this before anything sits in the sockets.

2. Primary forms: the brow and the jaw carry the expression

The brow ridge and the jawline do more work than any other two forms. They decide whether a face reads as heavy, sharp, tired or young, and they are visible from across a room. Detail passes cannot rescue a soft brow or a weak jaw - they can only decorate them.

The habit that helped most: sculpt the head, then flip it upside down. Errors in primary form are obvious when the face stops being recognisable as a face, and that check takes two seconds.

3. Secondary forms: where likeness actually lives

Cheekbones, the nasolabial fold, the shape of the eyelids, the plane change at the temple. This is the pass where a sculpt starts to look like a specific person rather than a generic head. It is also where patience matters most: the ClayBuildup brush at low intensity, working the planes rather than adding lumps.

4. Surface: pores last, and less than you think

Skin detail is the last five percent and the easiest to overdo. At the distances a head is usually seen, heavy pore passes read as noise. The surface pass is mostly about breaking up perfection: a few wrinkles where the face moves, slight asymmetry, and texture that follows the form rather than sitting on top of it.

5. Retopology is part of the sculpt

A sculpt that cannot be animated is a bust. Planning the edge loops while sculpting - around the eyes, the mouth, the jaw - costs nothing and saves a full retopo pass later. The ZRemesher guide brush does most of the work if the primary forms are clean.
